deliverables.text: A population-balance table: each district's total population, the statewide ideal (mean) district population, and each district's percent deviation from that ideal, for your chosen plan.

A compactness comparison with a labeled map: Polsby-Popper compactness score for the Treasure-Valley-anchored district under Plan A vs. the North Idaho region's shape under Plan B, using area/perimeter data and the area of a circle with matching perimeter as the benchmark, plus a convex/concave classification of each.

An efficiency-gap calculation: baseline efficiency gap for Idaho's current two-district map, and projected efficiency gap for your chosen plan's three-district map, apportioning any split county's votes by the same population share used to split its population.

balance.argument_a: Plan A (Whole Valley) keeps Ada+Canyon intact as District 3, honoring Idaho's stated preference to avoid county splits and producing the most compact, most convex District 3 achievable -- the traditional court-favored proxy against packing/cracking accusations, and the strongest defense against a 'this looks gerrymandered' visual challenge. Its real, computed weakness: District 3 alone is +18.44% over the statewide ideal district population (726,072 vs. 613,035), while Districts 1 and 2 land at -7.17% and -11.27%. Idaho's own 2021 Commission operated on a 5%-deviation-with-compelling-reason standard for legislative maps, and Karcher v. Daggett shows congressional courts scrutinize any deviation, however small, for a legitimate justification -- Plan A's defense rests entirely on 'county integrity is that legitimate justification,' a real, live legal argument, not a numeric tie.
balance.argument_b: Plan B (Balanced Split) sends a real, exactly-derived share of the Treasure Valley's population to each of the other two districts, bringing all three districts to within a few hundred people of the statewide ideal (613,035 each) -- directly serving the stricter one-person-one-vote standard Karcher applies to congressional maps, where Plan A's 18.44% deviation would need to survive judicial scrutiny that a near-0% deviation simply doesn't face. Its real, disclosed weakness: it requires splitting a county pair Idaho's own criteria say should stay whole 'wherever population math allows' -- and by Plan B's own logic, population math clearly does allow keeping them whole, just not at this population-equality level, so the split has to be justified on other grounds (rural/urban and statewide voting-bloc balance), not treated as unavoidable.
balance.margin_basis: Primary metric: absolute value of the statewide efficiency gap (%) on the projected 3-district map, computed via Appendix D/E's real district-level 2020 vote totals and Modeling Assumption MA2 (uniform statewide two-party vote share applied to every region). Under MA2, the projected efficiency gap is mathematically identical under Plan A and Plan B (~12.6%, computed from real vote totals) because vote share, not district population size, drives it under uniform swing -- so the two options are exactly tied on this specific metric by disclosed construction, forcing the discussion onto the two metrics that DO discriminate sharply: population deviation (D1, real: A=18.44% worst-district vs. B=~0%) and compactness/county-integrity (D2, real land-area/measured-perimeter dependent, A structurally favored). See FACILITATOR.md for how to run this without revealing D1/D2's real numbers as an answer key.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Exact geographic dividing line within the Treasure Valley for Plan B (only the population share sent to each district is fixed, not the precise line)
modeling_assumptions.value_used: ~6.1% of TV population to District 1, ~9.5% to District 2, ~84.4% remains District 3
modeling_assumptions.basis: No sub-county 2020 Census population data is reproduced in this case; the population-share targets are exactly derived (not guessed) from Appendix B's real county totals to bring District 1 and District 2 to the statewide ideal.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: D1's population-balance conclusion does not depend on where the line falls, only the population share. D2's compactness score and convex/concave classification depend heavily on the specific shape, which is why D2 requires the student to draw and defend their own version of the line.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Every region's 2020 U.S. House two-party vote share matches the statewide combined two-party vote share (68.7% / 31.3%) rather than a sourced county-level split
modeling_assumptions.value_used: Uniform statewide two-party split applied to all three regions for the projected efficiency gap
modeling_assumptions.basis: Idaho's own current two districts are already close to each other in vote share despite very different geography; full county-level precinct reprocessing (available via MIT Election Data and Science Lab) was outside this case's scope.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: This assumption makes the baseline efficiency gap real and correct (computed directly from real district-level results) but makes the *projected* efficiency gap identical under both plans by construction -- disclosed explicitly in case.json.balance and FACILITATOR.md, never in case.md as a revealed answer.

sensitivity_note: The Plan B population-share split of the Treasure Valley (Appendix F) is a stated Modeling Assumption, not a sourced fact -- case-research must state the assumed dividing line and justify it, and case-readiness's Tier 2 sensitivity probe should flex that share to confirm neither plan's argument depends on an unstated, precise split value.

context_glossary.desc: The process of redrawing electoral district boundaries, most often after a census, to reflect population change -- what Idaho's Commission for Reapportionment is doing here for the first time since gaining a third seat.

Drawing a district map to intentionally advantage or disadvantage a specific group, rather than to fairly represent the population within it -- the accusation both plans in this case are trying to avoid.
Concentrating a group of voters into as few districts as possible, so it wins those seats overwhelmingly but has no influence anywhere else.
Splitting a group of voters across multiple districts so their voting strength is diluted in all of them -- the opposite maneuver from packing.
A compactness measure that divides a district's actual land area by the area of a circle with the same perimeter -- the closer to 1.0, the more compact (circle-like) the shape.
A measure of partisan fairness that compares each side's "wasted votes" across every district in a map, divided by the total votes cast statewide.
Every vote that didn't change who won a district -- either cast for the losing candidate, or cast for the winner beyond the margin needed to win.

When a single county's population is divided between two or more districts instead of staying inside one -- something Idaho's own redistricting statute says should be avoided whenever the population math allows it.
Drawing two incumbents' districts into one, forcing them to run against each other -- a gerrymandering method distinct from packing or cracking a group of ordinary voters.
Redrawing a district so an incumbent's own home falls outside it, forcing them to run in unfamiliar territory or move.
A proposed legal standard holding that a given share of the statewide vote should produce the same share of legislative seats regardless of which party won that share.

The 2019 U.S. Supreme Court decision holding that partisan-gerrymandering claims are "political questions" -- meaning courts consider deciding them not their job, but instead a matter for the political branches -- so federal courts cannot rule on them, leaving state courts and state constitutions as the main remaining venue for that kind of challenge.

The Fourteenth Amendment provision requiring government bodies, including those drawing district maps, to treat people equally under the law -- the constitutional basis for requiring districts to have close to equal population.

A district requirement meaning every part of the district must connect to the rest of it -- no separate, disconnected pieces -- one of the basic shape rules a redistricting plan has to satisfy alongside compactness.
The person currently holding an elected office -- relevant here because some redistricting rules specifically forbid drawing districts to protect or target a sitting officeholder.
A 1965 federal law protecting against racial discrimination in voting, including a separate set of restrictions on drawing districts in ways that dilute the voting power of racial minority groups.

Groups of people who share common social, cultural, or economic interests -- a shared school district, industry, or neighborhood, for example -- that redistricting rules often say a map should try to keep together in one district where possible.
A group of voters who tend to vote the same way because they share a common interest or identity -- rural vs. urban is one example a commission has to weigh when balancing a district's population.
The constitutional principle that voting districts must have roughly equal population, so that one person's vote carries about the same weight as anyone else's, no matter which district they live in.
The smallest geographic unit elections are actually tallied in -- a city or county is divided into many precincts, each with its own polling place and vote count.

catalog.ask: Keep two counties whole, and the district looks compact and fair on a map -- but its population is wildly unbalanced. Split them instead, and the populations even out -- but the state's own rule against splitting counties gets broken. There may not be a clean answer here.
